observation_summary: The Closure Compiler fails to correctly rename function calls during optimization, leading to broken code where the function declaration is renamed but the corresponding call site is not, causing runtime errors.
hypothesis: The function inliner's logic for tracking and updating function references is flawed. It incorrectly identifies which nodes represent function calls that need to be tracked for renaming, leading to an incomplete update of function references.
prediction: The fix will involve changing the logic that identifies which nodes are tracked for renaming, likely by shifting from checking for CALL nodes to checking for NAME nodes that are valid candidates for inlining/renaming.
experiment_rationale: The fix diff shows a change in the logic that identifies nodes to be added to the 'changed' set. It replaces a check for CALL nodes with a check for NAME nodes that satisfy 'isCandidateUsage'. This confirms that the original algorithm for identifying function references was too restrictive or incorrectly targeted, failing to capture all necessary renaming points.
reasoning_summary: The bug is an algorithmic error in the function inliner's reference tracking logic. The compiler was failing to identify all instances of a function name that required renaming because it was only looking at CALL nodes. By changing the logic to identify candidate NAME nodes, the compiler correctly tracks all references. This is a procedural/algorithmic correction within the inlining pass, not a design-level capability gap (Function/Class/Object) or a simple value assignment (Assignment/Initialization).
evidence_used: The bug report states: 'Closure Compiler translates the name of the function in the declaration but not the call to the function.'
The fix diff shows: 'if (node.getType() == Token.CALL) { ... }' being replaced by 'if (node.getType() == Token.NAME) { if (isCandidateUsage(node)) { ... } }'
The fix modifies the logic for identifying which nodes are tracked for renaming.

alternative_types.why_not_primary: The issue is not a mismatch between two components' interfaces, but an internal failure of the compiler's inlining algorithm to correctly process the AST.
The capability to rename functions exists; the algorithm used to perform it is simply flawed in its implementation.
